label: From Classical to Modern Mechanics
notes: Welcome to Chapter 1, printed pages 11 through 36. We trace one bridge: from Newton and the variational principle, through the Legendre transform, to the symplectic form. By the close every Hamiltonian system will be a vector field that conserves energy and area, the seed of symplectic topology.

label: The Variational Principle
notes: Mechanics begins not with forces but with a single number, the action integral of the Lagrangian. Hamilton's principle says the realized path makes the action stationary. Setting the first variation to zero, and integrating by parts with fixed endpoints, produces the Euler-Lagrange equations governing every classical motion.

label: Euler-Lagrange Equations
notes: The Euler-Lagrange equation is the stationarity condition written coordinate by coordinate. It is a second-order system in the configuration variable q. For a particle in a potential it reproduces Newton's law exactly, confirming that the variational viewpoint loses nothing while gaining a coordinate-free, geometric formulation we will exploit.

label: The Legendre Transform
notes: To pass from velocities to momenta we apply the Legendre transform. The momentum p is the velocity-derivative of the Lagrangian, and the Hamiltonian is the corresponding convex dual. When this transform is invertible the velocity becomes a function of position and momentum, and the energy lands on phase space.

label: The Hamiltonian on Phase Space
notes: The Hamiltonian H of position and momentum is an energy landscape on the cotangent bundle, our phase space. Its level sets are the constant-energy hypersurfaces. The whole dynamical story now lives on this even-dimensional space, where a single function will generate the flow that classical forces once dictated.

label: Hamilton's Equations
notes: The second-order Euler-Lagrange system splits into a first-order pair: q-dot equals the p-derivative of H, p-dot equals minus the q-derivative of H. This symmetric coupling is Hamilton's equations. The minus sign is the source of every conservation law and the rotation we will see preserving phase area.

label: The Symplectic Form
notes: On Euclidean phase space we equip the manifold with the standard two-form omega, the sum of dp wedge dq over all degrees of freedom. It is closed and nondegenerate. Nondegeneracy means it identifies vectors with covectors; closedness will later guarantee that flows preserving it form a group.

label: Hamiltonian Vector Fields
notes: The symplectic form turns the differential of H into a vector field. The defining equation, omega contracted with X_H equals dH, has a unique solution because omega is nondegenerate. In standard coordinates X_H is exactly J times the gradient of H, recovering Hamilton's equations in compact geometric form.

label: Flow Tangent to Level Sets
notes: Because omega is antisymmetric, applying dH to X_H gives zero, so H is constant along its own flow. Geometrically the Hamiltonian vector field is everywhere tangent to the energy level sets. Energy conservation is not an accident here; it is forced by the antisymmetry of the symplectic form itself.

label: Symplectomorphisms Preserve Area
notes: A diffeomorphism that pulls omega back to itself is a symplectomorphism, the modern name for a canonical transformation. The central computation of the chapter shows that every Hamiltonian flow is symplectic, so it preserves omega and, in two dimensions, signed area. Liouville's theorem is the immediate corollary.

label: The Poisson Bracket
notes: The Poisson bracket pairs two observables into a third by feeding one through the Hamiltonian vector field of the other. It makes smooth functions a Lie algebra. A quantity is conserved exactly when its bracket with H vanishes, turning the search for constants of motion into pure bracket algebra.

label: First Global Questions
notes: Local theory is now complete, so we ask global questions. Must an area-preserving map of an annulus have fixed points? Must energy surfaces carry periodic orbits? These innocent-looking questions, unanswerable by local algebra, are exactly where symplectic topology begins and where the rest of the book lives.

label: Recap and Looking Ahead
notes: We assembled the bridge: action gives Euler-Lagrange, Legendre gives H, omega gives X_H, and the flow conserves energy and area. The Poisson bracket organizes conserved quantities. Next we leave Euclidean space, where rigidity phenomena like nonsqueezing show that symplectic maps are far stiffer than mere volume preservation.
